node.label: Jennifer S. H. Brown
node.date_label: Strangers in Blood 1980 · “Woman as Centre and Symbol in the Emergence of Metis Communities” 1983 · The New Peoples (ed. with Peterson) 1985 · The Orders of the Dreamed (with Brightman) 1988 · “Ethnohistorians: Strange Bedfellows, Kindred Spirits” 1991 · Reading Beyond Words (ed. with Vibert) 1996 · An Ethnohistorian in Rupert’s Land 2017
node.description: An anthropologist and historian of fur-trade families, the Métis, and Cree and Ojibwe history in the old Hudson's Bay Company territory. Strangers in Blood (1980) compared Hudson's Bay Company officers and North West Company partners as husbands and fathers; as a 1981 reviewer quoted it, the title took the British legal term for any relationship 'that the law refused to admit as legitimate' as 'one way of characterizing the meetings of Whites and Indians' in the fur trade. In 1983 she asked how women shaped Métis emergence, finding among North West Company fathers who had children baptized in Montreal that daughters were twice as likely as sons to stay in the Indian country, and in 1985 she co-edited with Jacqueline Peterson The New Peoples: Being and Becoming Métis in North America. As president of the American Society for Ethnohistory she spoke of 'our field, methodology, approach, or whatever it is we do when we do ethnohistory' (1991). A 1981 reviewer found the book weighed down by 'bits of anthropological theory'; Emma LaRocque (1999) placed her with Van Kirk in a 'neo cross-cultural approach', 'a much improved approach' on earlier work that still othered its subjects; and later scholarship rejects defining Métis by mixed descent, the biological starting point ('the meeting and mingling of Indian and white racial groups') that her 1983 essay set against a complex social history.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Jennifer S. H. Brown (b. 1940); doctoral study in anthropology at the University of Chicago, the dissertation revised as Strangers in Blood (per Brown 2012, 2017; dissertation unread); “A Demographic Transition in the Fur Trade Country” and “Changing Views of Fur Trade Marriage and Domesticity” (Western Canadian Journal of Anthropology, 1976); “Linguistic Solitudes and Changing Social Categories” (in Judd and Ray, eds., Old Trails and New Directions, 1980); Strangers in Blood: Fur Trade Company Families in Indian Country (Vancouver: UBC Press, 1980); “Children of the Early Fur Trades” (in Parr, ed., Childhood and Family in Canadian History, 1982); “Woman as Centre and Symbol in the Emergence of Metis Communities” (Canadian Journal of Native Studies, 1983); The New Peoples (ed. with Jacqueline Peterson, 1985), including her “Diverging Identities: The Presbyterian Métis of St. Gabriel Street, Montreal”; The Orders of the Dreamed: George Nelson on Cree and Northern Ojibwa Religion and Myth, 1823 (with Robert Brightman, 1988); “The Blind Men and the Elephant: Fur Trade History Revisited” (1990); “Ethnohistorians: Strange Bedfellows, Kindred Spirits” (Ethnohistory, 1991); Reading Beyond Words: Contexts for Native History (ed. with Elizabeth Vibert, 1996). After 2000: “Partial Truths: A Closer Look at Fur Trade Marriage” (2001); “‘All These Stories About Women’: ‘Many Tender Ties’ and a New Fur Trade History” (2012); An Ethnohistorian in Rupert’s Land: Unfinished Conversations (2017). Readings: Gresko (1981); Bowsfield (1981); Gagan and Turner (1982); LaRocque (1999); Fiske (2000); McPherson (2000). Later readings: Perry (2008); Gaudry (2013).
node.scope_note: Her own in-period words are read in 'Woman as Centre and Symbol in the Emergence of Metis Communities' (Canadian Journal of Native Studies 3:1, 1983, pp. 39–46, in full) and in an indexed excerpt only of her 1991 presidential address (Ethnohistory 38:2; OpenAlex's abstract field; p. 113 is the recorded first page, and the page itself was not inspected). Strangers in Blood and The New Peoples are not read: the Internet Archive copy of the 1980 book is borrow-only, and the 1985 collection is title-level. The book is quoted only as Gresko (1981) quotes it. An Ethnohistorian in Rupert's Land (2017, open access) was read in part: its acknowledgements, part introductions, chapter 3 and the opening of chapter 9 (reprints of 1990 and 1985 essays), and chapter 11 (her 2012 essay on Van Kirk). The 2017 reprints are labelled as later texts. The press notes that some chapter titles were modified, and chapter 3 cites a 2014 book, so the reprints do not witness the 1985 or 1990 wording. In-period readings read in full: Gresko (Canadian Woman Studies, 1981), Bowsfield (Archivaria, 1981), Gagan and Turner (Archivaria, 1982), LaRocque (1999, PDF p. 249), Fiske and McPherson (Atlantis, 2000). Later readings: Perry (2008), Gaudry (2013). She is not presented as a founder of Métis or fur-trade social history: her 1983 essay sets her questions beside Peterson's and Van Kirk's, and The New Peoples came from a 1981 Newberry Library conference that she helped organise. No identity classification is recorded for any critic named here.

proposed_edges.relationship: Company families compared, and women and descent in Métis emergence: Hudson's Bay and North West Company fathers, mothers and children (1980–85)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: In-period. Strangers in Blood (1980) is unread here. Gresko (Canadian Woman Studies 3:2, 1981, read in full) quotes the book's double sense of its title: the British legal term for 'any relationship, even familial that the law refused to admit as legitimate', and 'one way of characterizing the meetings of Whites and Indians ... in the fur trade of North America'. She reports that before 1821 the two companies, despite 'their common British (and heavily Scottish) facade', built different social organisations in Indian country. She quotes Brown that later social distinctions were 'strongly related to changing economic pressures' and that old Nor'Westers tended 'not to assume an active paternal role' (pp. 112–13). Bowsfield (Archivaria 12, 1981) singles out the 'comparison between Hudson's Bay Company and North West Company men as husbands and fathers', which Brown relates partly to 'the relationship of hinterland to metropolis' (p. 124). Her own words come from a paper to the Métis symposium held in Winnipeg in November 1982 (Canadian Journal of Native Studies 3:1, 1983, read in full). 'Biologically, métissage in North America can be described in a unitary way, as the meeting and mingling of Indian and white racial groups. Socially and culturally, it has had a complex history over many generations' (p. 40). Among Nor'Westers who had children baptized in Montreal, 1796–1821, sons were favoured 'by a margin of about two to one', so daughters 'were more likely by a two-to-one margin to remain in the Indian country, marrying there and contributing to the very rapid growth of biracial population' (p. 41). Coltman, Pambrun and McGillivray in 1818 'were all in accord in calling attention to the maternal element as formative in metis emergence' (p. 44). 'It is all too easy to learn more about the men than the women' (p. 45). The essay cites The New Peoples, then forthcoming from the 1981 Newberry Library Conference on the Metis; the 1985 collection itself is title-level here. Criticism. Gresko finds the book 'still too much in the form of the academic thesis' and 'complicated by seemingly insignificant bits of anthropological theory', and notes that it does not mention Jamieson's Indian Women and the Law in Canada (1978) (p. 113). LaRocque (1999, PDF p. 249) names Brown in the 'neo cross-cultural approach' that she criticises (see pe139_vankirk_rel_04 and edge_868). Not a founding: in 1983 she places her questions beside Jacqueline Peterson's (1981, 1982) and Van Kirk's (1980) (p. 40). Later readings, labelled. Gaudry (aboriginal policy studies 2:2, 2013, read in full) uses Peterson and Brown (1985) for the distinction between 'small-m métis', 'mixed Indigenous and European from a diversity of backgrounds', and 'big-M Métis', 'descended from the Red River Métis people, the New Nation'. With Andersen (2011, as Gaudry quotes him; unread), he rejects reducing 'the astonishing complexity of Red River Métis to their ostensible mixedness' (p. 78). He does not attribute that reduction to Peterson and Brown. In the 2017 reprint of her 1985 essay, Brown drops 'Presbyterian Métis' from the title. 'The term "Métis," as used in Rupert's Land in the 1800s, referred particularly to Roman Catholics of French Canadian paternal origin', and the children 'cannot be subsumed under any one label' (pp. 145–46).
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: fur_trade_families_metis ('company families (Brown) ... Peterson and Brown's collection treats Métis peoples in their own right (1985)') holds Brown and cites nnreq_brown_1980 and nnreq_peterson_brown_1985.

proposed_edges.relationship: Anthropological models brought to fur-trade, court and mission records for Métis, Cree and Ojibwe history (1983–96)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: In-period, her own words. The 1983 essay (Canadian Journal of Native Studies 3:1, read in full) reads fur-trade sources through anthropological models. Bishop and Krech's argument for early subarctic 'matriorganization' leads her to ask 'whether native women in emergent metis groups looked for and found ways to maintain this organizational bias in their own families and social lives' (p. 40). She tests Asch's 'unilocality' among the Slavey against fur-trade families (p. 42), using the HBC district report on Île-à-la-Crosse of 1823 (p. 42) and the published Red River testimonies of 1818 (pp. 43–44). She presents women's studies as 'one important perspective, among several' (p. 40). Her presidential address to the American Society for Ethnohistory (Ethnohistory 38:2, 1991) is known through an indexed excerpt only, OpenAlex's abstract field; the page itself was not inspected. It speaks of 'the rather obscure niche occupied by our field, methodology, approach, or whatever it is we do when we do ethnohistory', and offers 'auto-ethnohistory' as 'a useful handle for some reflections about ethnohistory and ethnohistorians, myself included' (indexed excerpt; p. 113 is the recorded first page). Title-level: The Orders of the Dreamed (with Brightman, 1988), an edition of the trader George Nelson's 1823 account of Cree and Northern Ojibwa religion and myth, and Reading Beyond Words: Contexts for Native History (ed. with Vibert, 1996). Reception, read in full: Fiske (Atlantis 25:1, 2000) cites Brown and Vibert (1996) for the literary turn 'that subjects both oral and written narratives to textual analysis' (p. 13). McPherson (2000, n. 31) cites an essay in that volume as discursive analysis of a Red River trial. Gresko (1981) objected to the 'bits of anthropological theory' in Strangers in Blood (p. 113). Later readings, labelled. Brown (2012, read in the 2017 reprint) recalls that 'my courses and professors directed me towards broader issues of method and theory'. She also says she 'benefited from confronting the multiple problems around defining such categories as "marriage," "custom," and "society"' (pp. 191–92). The 2017 part introduction calls the pair 'I coming from anthropology and Sylvia from history' (p. 159). Her essay 'The Blind Men and the Elephant' (1990) is read only in its revised 2017 reprint, which cites a 2014 book. There she asks historians to 'start by deconstructing' the fur trade, and warns that subsuming northern Native history under 'the fur trade era' restricts it to 'certain rather specialized "Indian-White relations"' (pp. 63–65); the 1990 wording is unchecked. The edge claims a contribution to the field's documentary method, not that she shaped ethnohistory as a whole.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: documentary_method ('Ethnological reading and documentary criticism': Lurie) is the closest strand: Brown reads company, court and mission documents with ethnological models. No strand covers the subarctic or Rupert's Land; archaeology_contact (Trigger) and collaboration_authority do not fit.

edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: Not proposed. Gagan and Turner (1982) and Fiske (2000) place her book beside Van Kirk's in the history of women, and in 1983 she wrote that 'women's studies provide one important perspective, among several'. But she has no roster row there; by her own later account her work 'focused more on Aboriginal history' (2012, p. 191); and an edge would retell Van Kirk's rel_02. The pair is shown once, as the comparison pe139_vankirk_rel_03.

Not proposed. Her Cree and Ojibwe work (The Orders of the Dreamed, 1988; the Berens River studies of the 1990s) is read only at title level or in 2017 reprints. The indigenous entry centres Indigenous historical traditions and authority, and LaRocque's criticism points the other way. The ethnohistory edge carries her method.

A lead, not proposed. In the 2017 reprint of 'The Blind Men and the Elephant' she writes that 'Canada has its fur trade thesis (or theses, if we allow for the multiple elaborations by historians and others from Harold Adams Innis onward)' and asks historians to deconstruct 'fur trade society' (pp. 61–63). The reprint is revised (it cites Conrad Black, 2014), and the 1990 Boreal Institute text was not read. If the 1990 text matches, a critique edge to Innis's strand could be proposed, dated 1988–90.
Not proposed. Her training is anthropological, but nothing read ties her work to a claim about the anthropology entry's strands. Ethnohistory is the better target.

verification.note: Read in full in an Internet Archive capture (22 October 2023) of the journal PDF (cws.journals.yorku.ca/index.php/cws/article/download/14091/13144); the live York site is behind a bot check. The PDF is a two-page scan whose OJS record is titled for the next review on the page (Posner, 'Becoming a Mother'); the article page gives Vol 3, No 2 (1981), Book Reviews, dated 1981-06-01. Printed '112' and '113' read on a 300-dpi re-OCR. Passages: 'any relationship, even familial that the law refused to admit as legitimate'; 'one way of characterizing the meetings of Whites and Indians ... in the fur trade of North America'; 'their common British (and heavily Scottish) facade'; 'strongly related to changing economic pressures'; 'not to assume an active paternal role'; 'still too much in the form of the academic thesis'; 'complicated by seemingly insignificant bits of anthropological theory'; no mention of Jamieson's Indian Women and the Law in Canada (1978). A same-reviewer Atlantis record (6:2, 1981, pp. 213–14, 'Strangers In Blood') was also checked: its PDF holds Gresko's review of Light and Strong-Boag's True Daughters of the North, not of Brown.

verification.note: Read in full in an Internet Archive capture (2016) of Brandon University's CJNS archive PDF; the live URL now returns 404. Running head 'THE CANADIAN JOURNAL OF NATIVE STUDIES III, 1(1983):39-46'; byline 'Department of Anthropology, University of Winnipeg'. The issue introduction says the papers were given at a Métis symposium in Winnipeg, 5–6 November 1982. OCR slips corrected ('coiling' to 'calling', 'contriburing' to 'contributing'). Passages: 'Biologically, métissage in North America can be described in a unitary way, as the meeting and mingling of Indian and white racial groups. Socially and culturally, it has had a complex history over many generations'; 'women's studies provide one important perspective, among several'; 'matriorganization'; 'Another starting point for this discussion is the work of Sylvia Van Kirk (1980)' (p. 40); 'patrifocality' (Brown 1980:218); 'by a margin of about two to one'; 'more likely by a two-to-one margin to remain in the Indian country' (p. 41); Asch's 'unilocality'; Île-à-la-Crosse 1823 (p. 42); 'were all in accord in calling attention to the maternal element as formative in metis emergence' (p. 44); 'It is all too easy to learn more about the men than the women' (p. 45). The references list Peterson and Brown, eds., The New Peoples, 'forthcoming', from the Newberry Library Conference on the Metis, Chicago, 1981.
